strengths: The paper provides a rigorous and creative mechanistic decomposition of pre-softmax attention logits into token-token (EE), token-position (EP/PE), and position-position (PP) components, and backs up the causal role of the EP term with targeted ablation experiments (zeroing specific terms and re-evaluating accuracy), which is a strong standard of evidence for the central mechanistic claim.

The controllable synthetic 1D testbed is well designed to isolate variables (label diversity vs. layout diversity) and cleanly demonstrates that label diversity is the primary driver of generalization to unseen object pairs — a concrete, useful empirical finding relevant to broader compositional generalization discussions.

Extending the analysis to RoPE (Appendix I) and deriving two distinct theoretical mechanisms (bias-induced positional gradient and learned subspace alignment) by which RoPE can induce the needed positional asymmetry is a valuable and non-trivial theoretical contribution connecting the toy findings to architectures used in modern LLMs/VLMs.

The paper is unusually thorough with extensive supporting appendices (dataset schematics, generalization dynamics/phases reminiscent of grokking, weight decay effects, head-pruning experiments, vision-text alignment via rotation, 2-layer extension) that substantially strengthen reproducibility and robustness of the claims within the toy setting.
The experimental setup (dataset generation, model hyperparameters, training details) is described with sufficient precision to be reproducible.
weaknesses: The core setting is an extremely simplified 1D, single-pixel-object, tiny-Transformer testbed; no experiments are conducted on real 2D images or actual pretrained CLIP models, so it remains unverified whether the identified EP-term mechanism operates in practice in real VLMs, which the paper itself only speculates about in the discussion.

The study focuses exclusively on a single relation type (left/right), which is a narrow slice of "spatial understanding" as advertised in the title/abstract; no evidence is given that the mechanism generalizes to other spatial relations (above/below, in front/behind, distance, etc.).

The clean, interpretable mechanistic story is fully established only for the maximally reduced 1-layer, LayerNorm/MLP-free model; once the architecture is scaled up even slightly (2-layer text encoder in Sec. 7, 2-layer vision encoder in Appendix L), the authors themselves note the mechanism becomes complex and only partially understood, weakening the generality of the central claim.

Even in the best-performing settings, unseen-pair generalization accuracy is well below 1 (e.g., ~0.86 for the 2-layer vision encoder, and near-chance in some ablations), and the paper does not fully explain the residual failure modes, limiting how completely the proposed mechanism accounts for observed behavior.

The paper does not compare against autoregressive VLM training paradigms despite explicitly motivating the work by their prevalence, leaving the claimed relevance to real-world VLM pipelines largely speculative.

Several key qualitative findings (e.g., Fig. 4b/5a attention patterns) are illustrated with single representative examples rather than systematically aggregated statistics with variance across many seeds/runs, which could raise concerns about cherry-picking, even though some quantitative aggregation is provided elsewhere (e.g., Fig. 4c, 5d).

strengths: The paper introduces a well-controlled, fully specified synthetic 1D image-text testbed that isolates left-right relational learning from confounds present in natural VLM training, enabling clean mechanistic analysis.

The attention logit decomposition (weight-bias, then token-position: EE/EP/PE/PP) is mathematically rigorous and clearly presented, and the causal ablation experiments (zeroing the EP and BP terms) convincingly demonstrate that a horizontal attention gradient arising from positional-token embedding interactions is necessary for left-right discrimination.

The mechanistic account is corroborated by multiple complementary lines of evidence: attention visualization, head-wise left/right bias statistics, ablation studies, a theoretical derivation (App. I) of when position-dependent asymmetry is required for OOD generalization, and an extension to RoPE with two distinct identified mechanisms (bias-induced gradient and learned subspace alignment).

Extensive supplementary analyses (label vs. layout diversity, weight decay/grokking-like dynamics, generalization phase transitions, head pruning, 2-layer extension, text-encoder attention analysis, rotation-based image-text token alignment) substantially strengthen the empirical support and show the authors probed robustness of their claims from many angles.

The work engages with an important and underexplored question (mechanistic origins of relational/spatial understanding in CLIP-style models) and connects clearly to prior literature on VLM compositional/spatial failures.
weaknesses: The setup is a highly simplified 1D, single-pixel-object synthetic environment; the paper explicitly acknowledges but does not empirically test whether the identified attention-gradient mechanism actually operates in real CLIP models trained on natural 2D images, so the practical significance/transferability of the central claim remains unverified.

No experiments connect the mechanistic findings back to real pretrained VLMs or existing spatial-reasoning benchmarks (e.g., ARO, Winoground, What's Up), leaving the link between the toy mechanism and observed real-world VLM spatial failures/successes largely speculative.

The two-representation setting (Sec. 7) is only partially resolved: the 1-layer text encoder fails to generalize and the mechanism by which a 2-layer text encoder discriminates XLY/XRY/YLX/YRX remains unexplained, leaving a central piece of the story (text-side discrimination with symmetric captions) incomplete.

Results are reported for what appear to be single training runs per configuration (no seed variance/error bars on main accuracy curves), making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of the reported trends, especially the more marginal unseen-pair generalization numbers (~0.8-0.9, not saturating).

The paper only studies left-right relations in one dimension; despite motivating the work with broader spatial/relational reasoning challenges (front/behind, inside/around, 2D layouts), no evidence is given that similar symmetry-breaking mechanisms would generalize to these richer relation types.

The mechanism identified (monotonic positional-embedding interaction breaking symmetry) is somewhat expected/intuitive given known properties of absolute positional embeddings in small transformers, which may temper the novelty relative to the paper's framing as a nontrivial mechanistic discovery.

strengths: Introduces a clean, fully controllable synthetic 1D image-text testbed with well-defined single-object positional, seen-pair configuration, and unseen-pair generalization metrics, enabling precise causal claims that are hard to make in natural-image VLMs.

Provides a rigorous mechanistic account: decomposing pre-softmax attention logits into EE/EP/PE/PP (and weight-bias) terms cleanly isolates the role of positional embeddings, and targeted ablations (zeroing specific logit terms) causally confirm that the EP cross-term (position-token interaction) is necessary for left-right discrimination, going beyond correlational attention visualization common in prior interpretability work.

Offers an accompanying theoretical analysis (Appendix J) deriving a precise consistency condition (|Π| ≫ |T|) under which position-dependent attention gradients must dominate token-dependent variation for OOD generalization to unseen object pairs, tying empirical findings to a principled argument.

Impressive breadth of robustness checks in the appendices: extension to RoPE (with two distinct identified mechanisms), 2D images, 3-object scenes, bidirectional (left+right) text supervision, autoregressive decoder-based VLM, head-pruning, and an approximate LayerNorm decomposition — collectively showing the phenomenon is not an artifact of the specific 1D/attention-only setup.

The empirical observation that label diversity (not layout/position diversity) drives generalization is a concrete, potentially actionable insight connecting to broader discussions of data diversity in compositional generalization.
Good reproducibility: explicit hyperparameters, compute budget, dataset construction procedure, and reference to public codebases used as a base.
weaknesses: The experimental setting is extremely reduced (1D sequences, single-pixel integer-coded 'objects', small vocabularies), so the vision encoder essentially learns token-identity plus positional embeddings rather than anything resembling real visual feature extraction; despite appendix extensions to 2D/3-object/RoPE, the core claims remain far removed from realistic VLM inputs, limiting confidence that the identified mechanism explains left-right understanding (or its absence) in large-scale trained CLIP models.

The paper is purely diagnostic/mechanistic and does not propose or validate any intervention that improves spatial reasoning in real, pretrained VLMs; the practical significance of the finding (attention gradients from positional embeddings encode left-right) is somewhat expected given how absolute positional embeddings function in Transformers, so the novelty is more in the careful demonstration than in a surprising discovery.

Several important phenomena are left unexplained or only partially characterized, e.g., the mechanism behind the sharp training-loss/accuracy phase transitions (Sec. 9/App. D), the interaction between multiple heads (App. P), and how signals propagate across layers (App. Q) — the authors acknowledge these as open questions, which is honest but also indicates the mechanistic account is only a 'first-order' one for a genuinely simplified regime.

No explicit statement of how many random seeds were used per experiment or variance across seeds for the main generalization curves, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of the accuracy curves and ablation percentages (e.g., Table 2/3 percentages appear to be single-run numbers).

The manuscript is very appendix-heavy (39 pages) relative to the main text; while thorough, this places a large burden on the reader to verify the central claims, and some of the extensions (RoPE theory, LayerNorm 9-term decomposition) are dense and only partially validated ('a thorough validation ... is left for future work').

The link between this toy-model finding and the well-documented failure of real large-scale CLIP models on relational/compositional benchmarks (e.g., ARO, Winoground) is asserted rather than empirically tested — the paper does not attempt to verify whether the identified attention-gradient mechanism is present, weak, or absent in actual trained CLIP checkpoints on natural images.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and underexplored question: not just whether VLMs succeed or fail at spatial relations, but the mechanistic origin of any relational competence they do acquire, complementing a large literature of purely evaluative benchmarks (ARO, Winoground, CLEVR, etc.).

The controllable synthetic 1D image-text testbed is carefully designed with clear, well-motivated definitions of three distinct generalization types (single-object positional, seen-pair configuration, unseen-pair), and a clean train/test split that avoids leakage (Fig. 9).

The core mechanistic finding—that a horizontal attention gradient arising specifically from the interaction between positional and token embeddings (the EP cross term) is necessary and causally responsible for left-right discrimination—is derived through a principled weight-bias/token-position logit decomposition and validated via targeted ablations that quantitatively degrade unseen-pair accuracy to chance (Fig. 5e, Sec. 5), which is a rigorous standard of evidence rather than mere correlational attention-map inspection.

Extensive robustness checks are provided across many axes: 2D images (App. K), 3-object scenes (App. N), autoregressive decoder-based VLMs (App. O), RoPE positional encoding with a full theoretical derivation of two distinct generalization mechanisms (App. J), LayerNorm/MLP inclusion (App. R), multi-head pruning (App. P), and deeper 2-layer models (App. Q) — this breadth substantially strengthens the claim that the identified mechanism is not an artifact of one narrow simplified setting.

The finding that label diversity (not layout diversity) drives generalization is a clear, interesting empirical result connected meaningfully to related work on data diversity and compositional generalization (Uselis et al. 2025), with a plausible mechanistic interpretation of the difference (positional comparison vs. additive factorization).

The theoretical analysis in App. J deriving a consistency condition for OOD generalization under both learnable positional embeddings and RoPE, and confirming it empirically (Fig. 19), adds valuable analytical depth beyond purely empirical demonstration.

The paper is transparent about compute resources, codebases, and hyperparameters (App. B), aiding reproducibility, and the discussion section honestly flags open questions (multi-head interactions, layer propagation, non-linear component analysis) rather than overclaiming completeness.
weaknesses: The core setting is a highly simplified 1D synthetic testbed with small vocabularies, single pixels per object, and shallow (1-2 layer) Transformers; while several extensions are provided, the central mechanistic claims are primarily demonstrated in this minimal regime, and it remains unproven whether the identical EP-term attention-gradient mechanism is the dominant driver of left-right competence in large-scale, deep, pretrained CLIP models on natural images (the paper acknowledges this as future work but the gap is substantial given how much architectural and data complexity is abstracted away).

The phase-transition/grokking-like dynamics (Fig. 11) and the mechanism behind the loss discontinuity at the phase-1/phase-2 boundary are noted but left unexplained ("underlying mechanism remains unclear at present"), which is a real limitation on the completeness of the mechanistic story despite being honestly disclosed.

Some quantitative results have only modest sample support behind visual claims (e.g., single attention-map examples in Figs. 4b, 6a are used as representative illustrations of general patterns, though aggregate statistics like Fig. 4c partially mitigate this).

The extension to autoregressive VLMs (App. O) uses frozen, randomly initialized vision token embeddings and a minimal decoder, which is a considerably more artificial setup than typical autoregressive VLM training, limiting how much can be concluded about mechanism-transfer to realistic autoregressive VLMs beyond a proof-of-concept.

The 3-object extension (App. N) shows only partial transfer (2-object-trained models achieve just 15% on "3obj top-3 all"), and while direct 3-object training helps, performance is still not saturated (e.g., 56-58% top-1 for the 1-layer text encoder case), suggesting the simple left/right binary mechanism may not straightforwardly scale to richer relational structures with more objects.

The LayerNorm decomposition in App. R is explicitly called "approximate" and only analyzed for the first layer; extending the exact mechanistic account to genuinely non-linear, deep, multi-layer models (which is where practical VLMs operate) remains unaddressed, so the causal/ablation-based rigor achieved in the toy attention-only setting is not yet matched in more realistic architectures.
